description: The Sun is a G-type main-sequence star, the yellow dwarf at the gravitational heart of the Solar System and the yardstick against which every other star here is measured. It is seeded at the origin because the whole map is heliocentric: distances, brightnesses and radii are all quoted relative to it (R☉, L☉, M☉). About 4.6 billion years old and roughly halfway through its hydrogen-burning life, it fuses some 600 million tonnes of hydrogen every second at a core temperature near 15 million K. It has no constellation of its own — from Earth it appears to drift along the ecliptic through the zodiac over the course of a year.

Proxima Centauri is the closest star to the Sun, a diminutive red dwarf about 1.30 parsecs (4.25 light-years) away in the constellation Centaurus. Its name is simply Latin for 'nearest', and it is the outermost, gravitationally bound third member of the Alpha Centauri system, orbiting the bright A–B pair once in roughly 550,000 years. Barely a seventh the mass of the Sun and thousands of times fainter, it is a UV Ceti-type flare star whose brightness can jump dramatically when magnetic outbursts erupt from its surface. It hosts at least one planet, the roughly Earth-mass Proxima b, which orbits within the star's habitable zone — making it the nearest known exoplanet to Earth.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Alpha Centauri A, the Sun-like G2V primary; SIMBAD 'alf Cen A' lists no Gaia DR3 row (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Alpha Centauri is the nearest stellar system to the Sun and, at apparent magnitude near zero, the third-brightest star in the night sky. What the eye sees as a single point is really a close binary of two Sun-like stars — the G2 primary Rigil Kentaurus (component A) and the slightly cooler K1 dwarf Toliman (component B) — orbiting each other every 80 years, with the red dwarf Proxima as a distant third companion. Component A is almost a twin of our own Sun in mass, temperature and colour, which makes the system a favourite target for imagining nearby habitable worlds. Its estimated age is debated, with determinations ranging from roughly 5 to 8 billion years.

Barnard's Star is a faint red dwarf in Ophiuchus and, after the Alpha Centauri system, the closest individual star to the Sun. It is famous for having the largest proper motion of any known star: measured by E. E. Barnard in 1916, it races across our sky at more than 10 arcseconds a year, covering a full lunar diameter roughly every 180 years. An ancient, metal-poor star perhaps 10 billion years old, it is too dim to see without a telescope despite its proximity. Decades of planet-hunting finally paid off in 2024–25 with the confirmation of several sub-Earth-mass planets circling it.

Wolf 359 is one of the smallest and faintest stars known in the Sun's immediate neighbourhood, a cool red dwarf in Leo just under 2.4 parsecs away. With barely a tenth of the Sun's mass and about a thousandth of its luminosity, it sits close to the lower limit of how small a hydrogen-fusing star can be. It is a UV Ceti-type flare star (catalogued as the variable CN Leonis), prone to sudden brightenings driven by intense magnetic activity. Its proximity has made it a fixture of science fiction, most famously as the site of a pivotal battle in Star Trek: The Next Generation.

Lalande 21185 is a red dwarf in Ursa Major, catalogued from the star charts of the 18th-century French astronomer Jérôme Lalande. Although still far too faint for the naked eye, it is the brightest red dwarf in the northern sky and one of the closest stars to the Sun at about 2.5 parsecs. Roughly 40% of the Sun's mass and an old star some 8 billion years old, it shows the high proper motion typical of nearby stars. Precise radial-velocity monitoring has revealed at least two planets orbiting it, both more massive than Earth.

gaiaDr3Note: Sirius A; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among its identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Sirius, the Dog Star of Canis Major, is the brightest star in the night sky, blazing at apparent magnitude −1.46 — a distinction it owes both to its intrinsic luminosity and to its closeness, just 2.6 parsecs away. Its name comes from the Greek Seirios, meaning 'scorching' or 'glowing', and its heliacal rising once marked the flooding of the Nile for the ancient Egyptians. The bright star we see is Sirius A, a hot blue-white A-type star about twice the Sun's mass; it is orbited every 50 years by Sirius B, a faint but extraordinarily dense white dwarf that was the first such star ever discovered. Together with Procyon and Betelgeuse, Sirius forms the Winter Triangle.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents the Luyten 726-8 system, resolved to primary component A (BL Ceti / GJ 65 A); the companion is UV Ceti.
description: Luyten 726-8 is a close binary of two nearly identical red dwarfs in Cetus, about 2.7 parsecs away, discovered by the prolific proper-motion cataloguer Willem Luyten. Both stars are tiny, cool M dwarfs near the bottom of the main sequence, and both are vigorous flare stars. Its component B, UV Ceti, is the prototype of the entire class of UV Ceti-type flare stars — dwarfs that can brighten by a magnitude or more in seconds during magnetic eruptions. Component A carries the variable-star name BL Ceti and is the one whose position anchors this entry.

Ross 154 is a nearby red dwarf in Sagittarius, one of the many high-proper-motion stars catalogued by the American astronomer Frank Elmore Ross in the 1920s. Lying about 3 parsecs from the Sun, it is a young, magnetically active M dwarf and a UV Ceti-type flare star, carrying the variable designation V1216 Sagittarii. Its flares are frequent, with major outbursts separated on average by only a couple of days. With less than a fifth of the Sun's mass, it shines at barely four-thousandths of the Sun's luminosity.

Ross 248 is a faint red dwarf in Andromeda, another discovery from Frank Ross's proper-motion surveys, sitting about 3.2 parsecs away. It is a small, cool M dwarf whose brightness varies slightly as star-spots rotate across its face, earning it the BY Draconis-type variable name HH Andromedae. Its chief claim to fame lies in the future: because it is moving toward the Solar System, in roughly 36,000 years Ross 248 will briefly become the closest star to the Sun, displacing the Alpha Centauri system for several thousand years. The Voyager 2 spacecraft is loosely headed in its general direction.

Epsilon Eridani, formally named Ran, is a young orange K-type dwarf in the constellation Eridanus and one of the closest Sun-like stars, about 3.2 parsecs away and easily visible to the naked eye. Younger and cooler than the Sun, it is magnetically active and encircled by at least one debris disk, a dusty analogue of our own asteroid and Kuiper belts. Its proximity and Sun-like character made it a target of Project Ozma, the first modern search for radio signals from other civilisations, back in 1960. A confirmed giant planet, Epsilon Eridani b (named AEgir), orbits within the system.

Lacaille 9352 is a red dwarf in Piscis Austrinus, catalogued by the 18th-century French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille during his survey of the southern sky. At about 3.3 parsecs it is among the nearest stars, and with roughly half the Sun's mass it is one of the brighter, more massive red dwarfs in the solar neighbourhood. It has the fourth-highest proper motion of any known star, sweeping across nearly seven arcseconds of sky each year. A quiet, comparatively bright M dwarf, it hosts a compact family of confirmed planets, one of which lies in its habitable zone.

Ross 128 is a nearby red dwarf in Virgo, discovered by Frank Ross and lying about 3.4 parsecs from the Sun. Although catalogued as the flare star FI Virginis, it is unusually quiet and magnetically settled for a red dwarf, a sign of its middle age. In 2017 it drew attention as the host of Ross 128 b, a roughly Earth-mass planet in a temperate orbit — at the time the second-closest known Earth-size world beyond the Solar System. Its relatively calm activity makes that planet a comparatively promising place to look for benign conditions.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents the EZ Aquarii triple system, resolved to primary component A (GJ 866 A).
description: EZ Aquarii is a remarkable triple system of red dwarfs in Aquarius, about 3.5 parsecs away, also catalogued as Luyten 789-6. Its three stars are all tiny, cool M dwarfs; two of them orbit each other in a tight inner pair every eleven days, with the third circling that pair every few years. The whole system is a UV Ceti-type flare star, prone to sudden magnetic brightenings, and carries the variable name EZ Aquarii. Because its components are so low in mass and luminosity, the entire system is far too faint to be seen without a telescope despite its closeness.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents 61 Cygni A (K5V), the primary of this wide binary; component B is a cooler K7 dwarf.
description: 61 Cygni is a wide binary of two orange K-type dwarfs in Cygnus, about 3.5 parsecs away, and holds a special place in the history of astronomy. In 1838 Friedrich Bessel used its large parallax to make the first successful measurement of the distance to any star beyond the Sun, earning it the nickname 'Bessel's Star'. Its exceptional proper motion had already flagged it as a nearby object; Giuseppe Piazzi called it the 'Flying Star'. Today it remains the star with the highest proper motion still visible to the unaided eye, its two components orbiting each other over roughly 680 years.

gaiaDr3Note: Procyon A; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among its identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Procyon is the brightest star in the small constellation Canis Minor and the eighth-brightest in the entire night sky, at apparent magnitude 0.34. Its name comes from the Greek for 'before the dog', because it rises just ahead of Sirius, the Dog Star, as the sky turns. Like Sirius, it is a bright, nearby star with a white-dwarf companion: Procyon A is a yellow-white F-type star beginning to swell as it exhausts its core hydrogen, orbited every 40 years by the faint Procyon B. It forms the third vertex of the Winter Triangle alongside Sirius and Betelgeuse.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Struve 2398 A (GJ 725 A), the primary of a red-dwarf binary; both components are flare stars.
description: Struve 2398 is a binary of two red dwarfs in Draco, about 3.6 parsecs away, named for the entry it holds in the double-star catalogue of Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve. Both stars are modest M dwarfs of similar size, orbiting their common centre of mass over several centuries. Each is a flare star, subject to the sudden magnetic brightenings common among active red dwarfs. This entry stands for the brighter primary, component A (also known as GJ 725 A), which anchors the pair's position on the sky.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Groombridge 34 A (GX Andromedae / GJ 15 A), the primary of a red-dwarf binary; both components are flare stars.
description: Groombridge 34 is a pair of red dwarfs in Andromeda, about 3.6 parsecs away, taken from a star catalogue compiled by the English astronomer Stephen Groombridge in the early 19th century. Its two components, the flare stars GX Andromedae and GQ Andromedae, are both small, dim M dwarfs invisible to the naked eye. The brighter primary, component A (GJ 15 A), hosts at least two confirmed planets, including a super-Earth in a short orbit. This entry represents that primary, which fixes the system's place on the sky.

gaiaDr3Note: Resolved to Epsilon Indi A (HD 209100), the K-dwarf primary; the system also contains a brown-dwarf binary (Ba/Bb).
description: Epsilon Indi is a nearby orange K-type dwarf in the southern constellation Indus, about 3.6 parsecs away and comfortably visible to the naked eye. Smaller and cooler than the Sun, it is a relatively quiet star notable for its rich retinue of companions. Circling the main star at a great distance is a pair of brown dwarfs, Epsilon Indi Ba and Bb — one of the closest known brown-dwarf systems to the Sun. A giant planet, Epsilon Indi Ab, several times the mass of Jupiter, was later confirmed on a wide, long-period orbit.

Tau Ceti is a single G-type star in Cetus, about 3.65 parsecs away, and the closest solitary Sun-like star to the Solar System after Alpha Centauri A. Slightly smaller and cooler than the Sun and notably poor in heavy elements, it is an old, stable, magnetically calm star — qualities that have long made it a touchstone in the search for life. In 1960 it was one of the two original targets of Project Ozma, and it recurs throughout science fiction as a plausible destination. It is surrounded by a substantial debris disk, and several planet candidates have been proposed, though none is yet unambiguously confirmed.

Kapteyn's Star is a red subdwarf in the southern constellation Pictor, about 3.9 parsecs away, discovered in 1898 by the Dutch astronomer Jacobus Kapteyn. It is the closest known halo star to the Sun — an ancient, metal-poor member of the Milky Way's Population II — and it orbits the Galaxy backwards, retrograde to the disk's rotation, probably having been stripped from a dwarf galaxy long ago. When discovered it held the record for the highest proper motion of any star, later surpassed by Barnard's Star. At around 11 billion years old, it is one of the oldest stars in the solar neighbourhood.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD 'Altair' lists no Gaia DR3 source among its identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Altair is the brightest star in the constellation Aquila, the Eagle, and one of the nearest bright stars at just over 5 parsecs; its name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the flying eagle'. A hot white A-type star, it forms the southern vertex of the Summer Triangle together with Vega and Deneb. Altair spins extraordinarily fast, completing a rotation in under nine hours, which flattens it into a visibly oblate spheroid whose equator is more than a fifth wider than its poles. In 2007 it became the first main-sequence star other than the Sun to have its surface directly imaged, revealing that flattening and the temperature difference between its cooler equator and hotter poles.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD 'Vega' lists no Gaia DR3 source among its identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Vega is the brightest star in the constellation Lyra and the fifth-brightest in the night sky, a hot blue-white A-type star about 7.7 parsecs away. It served for over a century as the anchor of the photometric magnitude scale, the star against which the brightness of others was defined at magnitude zero. Because of the slow precession of Earth's axis, Vega was the northern pole star around 12,000 BCE and will be again in roughly 13,700 CE. Like Altair it is a rapid rotator, seen nearly pole-on, and it was one of the first stars found to be surrounded by a dusty debris disk — the archetype of the 'Vega-like' disks.

gaiaDr3Note: Fomalhaut A; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among its identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Fomalhaut is the brightest star in Piscis Austrinus, the Southern Fish, and a lonely beacon of the autumn sky often called the 'Solitary One' because it has few bright neighbours; its name derives from Arabic for 'the mouth of the fish'. A young, hot A-type star about 7.7 parsecs away, it is encircled by a strikingly sharp-edged ring of dusty debris that has made it a showcase for studies of planetary systems in formation. An object imaged within that ring, Fomalhaut b, was hailed as one of the first exoplanets seen directly in visible light, though later observations showed it to be an expanding cloud of debris from a colossal collision rather than a planet.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD 'Pollux' lists no Gaia DR3 source among its identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Pollux is the brightest star in Gemini and, despite its Beta designation, outshines its neighbour Castor; the two mark the heads of the mythological twins the constellation is named for. It is an orange giant about 10 parsecs away, a star that has exhausted the hydrogen in its core and swollen to nearly nine times the Sun's diameter. That makes it the nearest giant star to the Solar System. In 2006 it became one of the first giant stars confirmed to host a planet — Pollux b, later formally named Thestias — a gas giant a few times the mass of Jupiter.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Canopus — a saturated bright-star hole.
description: Canopus is the second-brightest star in the night sky and the brightest in the southern constellation Carina, the Keel of the ancient ship Argo. Despite lying about 95 parsecs away — far more distant than most first-magnitude stars — it shines at magnitude −0.74 because it is an intrinsically luminous yellow-white supergiant, roughly ten thousand times brighter than the Sun. Its name has long been linked to a navigator of the Greek fleet at Troy, and today spacecraft use it as a guide star for attitude control. It is a rare A-type bright giant fusing helium in its core, on its way to ending as a massive white dwarf.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Arcturus — a saturated bright-star hole.
description: Arcturus is the brightest star in the constellation Boötes and the brightest in the entire northern celestial hemisphere, a warm orange giant just 11.3 parsecs away. Its name comes from the Greek for 'guardian of the bear', as it appears to follow Ursa Major around the pole; skywatchers find it by 'arcing to Arcturus' along the curved handle of the Big Dipper. Having exhausted the hydrogen in its core, it has swollen to some 25 times the Sun's diameter and shines around 170 times as brightly. It belongs to the Milky Way's older thick-disk population and moves on an unusual path, part of a stream of stars that share its motion through the Galaxy.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Capella Aa, the primary yellow giant; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for the combined bright star (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Capella is the brightest star in the constellation Auriga, the Charioteer, and the sixth-brightest in the night sky; its name is Latin for 'little she-goat'. What looks like a single golden star is really two yellow giants orbiting each other every 104 days, so close together that no telescope resolves them directly. The primary is a cool giant nearly twelve times the Sun's radius, paired with a slightly hotter, more compact companion, and a distant duo of red dwarfs accompanies the pair. At just 13 parsecs away, it is the nearest first-magnitude star to the north celestial pole.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Rigel A (β Ori A), the blue supergiant primary; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Rigel is a brilliant blue supergiant marking the left foot of Orion the Hunter and, despite its Beta designation, usually the brightest star in the constellation. Its name derives from the Arabic for 'the foot', and at roughly 260 parsecs it pours out around 120,000 times the Sun's light. Rigel is the luminous primary of a multiple system, with a fainter companion resolvable in small telescopes that is itself a close pair of stars. It pulsates slightly as an Alpha Cygni-type variable and is destined to end its brief life as a supernova.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Achernar — a saturated bright-star hole.
description: Achernar is the brightest star in Eridanus, the River, and the ninth-brightest in the night sky, its name meaning 'the river's end' in Arabic. A hot blue main-sequence star about 43 parsecs away, it is the flattest star known in the Milky Way: it spins so fast — near the speed at which it would fly apart — that its equatorial diameter is more than half again its polar diameter. This furious rotation flings gas off the equator into a circumstellar disk, giving the star its emission-line 'e' classification. A smaller, hotter companion orbits it closely.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among Betelgeuse's identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Betelgeuse is the red supergiant marking the shoulder of Orion, one of the largest and most luminous stars visible to the naked eye; placed at the Sun's position, its bloated surface would swallow the orbit of Mars and beyond. Its name derives from an Arabic phrase for the hand or armpit of the giant, and it glows a distinctive deep orange-red at a surface temperature only about half the Sun's. As a semiregular variable it fluctuates in brightness, and its dramatic 'Great Dimming' of 2019–2020 — later traced to a cloud of dust the star had ejected — fuelled speculation that it might be about to explode. It is indeed nearing the end of its life and will one day detonate as a supernova, briefly rivalling the Moon in our sky.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents the massive B-type primary of the Hadar (β Cen) system; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Hadar, also called Agena, is the second-brightest star in Centaurus and the eleventh-brightest in the sky, forming with nearby Alpha Centauri a pair of 'Southern Pointers' that guide observers to the Southern Cross. It is a hot blue giant about 120 parsecs away, far more distant and intrinsically far more luminous than its bright neighbour. Hadar is in fact a triple system: the main object is itself two nearly identical massive B-type stars in a tight, eccentric orbit, with a third star circling farther out. Its component stars pulsate slightly as Beta Cephei-type variables.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Acrux α¹ Cru, the brighter component; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for the bright pair (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Acrux is the brightest star in Crux, the Southern Cross, and the thirteenth-brightest in the sky; marking the foot of the cross, it is the most southerly first-magnitude star, invisible from most of the northern hemisphere. Its name is simply a contraction of 'Alpha Crucis'. Through a telescope it splits into two brilliant blue stars, and each of those is in turn a spectroscopic binary of hot, massive, short-lived B-type stars. The whole group is only a few million years young and belongs to the Scorpius–Centaurus association of recently formed stars.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Aldebaran — a saturated bright-star hole.
description: Aldebaran is the brightest star in Taurus and marks the fiery red eye of the celestial bull, glaring out from amid the V-shaped Hyades cluster — though it lies only about 20 parsecs away, less than half the distance of that background cluster and quite unrelated to it. Its name comes from the Arabic for 'the follower', because it appears to chase the Pleiades across the sky. An ageing orange giant some 45 times the Sun's diameter, it has cooled and swelled after exhausting the hydrogen in its core. NASA's Pioneer 10 spacecraft is drifting in its general direction and will pass near it in roughly two million years.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Antares A (α Sco A), the red supergiant primary; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Antares is the brightest star in Scorpius and marks the heart of the scorpion, a colossal red supergiant whose fiery hue earned it the Greek name meaning 'rival of Ares' — a rival of Mars, the red planet it superficially resembles. Lying roughly 170 parsecs away, it is several hundred times the Sun's diameter and, like Betelgeuse, would engulf the inner planets were it set at the Sun's position. It has a hot blue companion, Antares B, normally lost in the supergiant's glare but glimpsed during lunar occultations, when it can appear faintly green by contrast. A slow irregular variable nearing the end of its life, Antares too is a future supernova.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among Spica's identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Spica is the brightest star in Virgo and the fifteenth-brightest in the night sky, its name Latin for 'the ear of wheat' held by the maiden the constellation represents. What appears as a single blue-white star is a very close binary of two hot, massive stars circling each other in just four days, so near that their mutual gravity distorts them into egg shapes. This distortion makes the system a rotating ellipsoidal variable, its light rippling slightly as the elongated stars turn, while the primary also pulsates. Lying about 77 parsecs away, both stars are massive enough that the primary is expected to end as a supernova.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among Deneb's identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Deneb is the brightest star in Cygnus, the Swan, and marks the swan's tail — the meaning of its Arabic-derived name — as well as the head of the Northern Cross and one vertex of the Summer Triangle. It is a white supergiant of extraordinary intrinsic power, radiating on the order of 100,000 times the Sun's light; although its exact distance is hard to pin down, it lies perhaps 800 parsecs away, by far the most remote of the very brightest stars. It is the prototype of the Alpha Cygni class of pulsating variables, whose surfaces heave in overlapping, non-radial waves. Having burned through the hydrogen in its enormous core, Deneb is fated to explode as a supernova within a few million years.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Mimosa — a saturated bright-star hole.
description: Mimosa, also known as Becrux, is the second-brightest star in the Southern Cross and the twentieth-brightest in the sky, a hot blue giant about 85 parsecs away. It is one of the hottest naked-eye stars, with a surface near 27,000 K, and it pulsates in a matter of hours as a Beta Cephei-type variable. A massive companion orbits it on a highly elongated five-year path. Only a few million years old, it belongs to the same young Scorpius–Centaurus association as many of the bright blue stars of the southern sky.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Regulus A (α Leo A), the primary; SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Regulus is the brightest star in Leo and marks the heart of the celestial lion; its name is Latin for 'little king', echoing an ancient association with royalty. It is a hot blue-white star about 24 parsecs away that spins astonishingly fast, completing a rotation in under sixteen hours — near the speed at which it would tear itself apart — so that it bulges markedly at the equator while its poles shine hotter and brighter than its cooler equatorial regions. Regulus is the senior member of a system of at least four stars, closely accompanied by a faint white-dwarf companion and, much farther out, by a pair of dim orange and red dwarfs. Sitting almost exactly on the ecliptic, it is regularly occulted by the Moon.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Adhara A (ε CMa A), the bright giant primary; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Adhara is the second-brightest star in Canis Major, outshone only by Sirius; its Arabic-derived name means 'the virgins'. It is a hot blue bright giant about 130 parsecs away with a faint companion, and it ranks among the most powerful sources of extreme-ultraviolet radiation in the entire sky. Around 4.7 million years ago Adhara passed within roughly 10 light-years of the Sun and would then have blazed as the brightest star in Earth's sky, at nearly magnitude −4. No star is expected to appear that bright to terrestrial observers again for millions of years.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Castor Aa, the brightest component of the sextuple system; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for the bright pair (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Castor is the second-brightest star in Gemini and, with neighbouring Pollux, represents the heads of the mythological twins the constellation is named for. To the eye it is a single point about 15 parsecs away, but it is really a remarkable family of six stars: two bright A-type stars, each shadowed by a close red-dwarf companion, orbit one another, while a fainter, wider pair of red dwarfs circles the whole group. All six are gravitationally bound, making Castor one of the nearest and best-studied sextuple systems. The two dominant white stars can be split in a modest telescope.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Shaula A (λ Sco A), the primary; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Shaula is the second-brightest star in Scorpius, marking the raised stinger at the tip of the scorpion's tail — a position captured by its Arabic-derived name, 'the raised tail'. Lying about 175 parsecs away, it is a hot blue subgiant that pulsates in a few hours as a Beta Cephei-type variable. Shaula is a triple system: the bright star has a close companion and a wider one, and the innermost object is unusually hot and dense, possibly a young pre-main-sequence star or an exotic compact remnant. Together with nearby Lesath it forms a striking pair sometimes called the 'Cat's Eyes' of the scorpion.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Gacrux — a saturated bright-star hole.
description: Gacrux is the top star of the Southern Cross and, at about 27 parsecs, the nearest red giant to the Sun. Its name is a modern contraction of 'Gamma Crucis'. Cool and swollen to roughly 120 times the Sun's diameter, it glows a deep orange-red that contrasts vividly with the hot blue-white stars forming the rest of the cross. A much fainter white star lies along the same line of sight and can be seen with binoculars, but it is a chance alignment rather than a true companion. Gacrux has dredged material up from its interior, enriching its atmosphere with the element barium.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Bellatrix — a saturated bright-star hole.
description: Bellatrix marks the left shoulder of Orion and is the third-brightest star in the constellation; its Latin name means 'the female warrior', and it is sometimes called the Amazon Star. A hot blue giant about 77 parsecs away, it is one of the nearer luminous B-type stars and shines around nine thousand times as brightly as the Sun. Because its brightness sits close to a value once used as a reference on the magnitude scale, it has long served astronomers as a photometric standard. Having consumed the hydrogen in its core, it is evolving toward a cooler, more swollen future as a giant.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Elnath — a saturated bright-star hole.
description: Elnath marks the tip of the northern horn of Taurus, the bull, and is the constellation's second-brightest star after Aldebaran; its Arabic-derived name means 'the butting', evoking the goring horn. It sits on the border with Auriga and carries a second Bayer label, Gamma Aurigae, a relic of the days when Ptolemy shared it between the two figures before modern constellation boundaries assigned it to Taurus. It is a hot blue-white giant about 41 parsecs away, and a chemically peculiar one, its atmosphere showing unusually strong lines of manganese and other heavy elements. Having begun to evolve off the main sequence, it now shines several hundred times as brightly as the Sun.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Miaplacidus — a saturated bright-star hole.
description: Miaplacidus is the second-brightest star in Carina, the keel of the old ship Argo Navis, and the brightest member of the Diamond Cross asterism. Its curious name blends the Arabic word for 'waters' with the Latin for 'placid', a hybrid that first appeared on star maps in the nineteenth century. Lying about 35 parsecs away, it is a white giant that has exhausted the hydrogen in its core and swelled to nearly six times the Sun's diameter. It spins fairly rapidly, at around 150 kilometres per second, and lies near the planetary nebula IC 2448.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among Alnilam's identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Alnilam is the central and most distant of the three stars forming Orion's Belt, its Arabic-derived name meaning 'the string of pearls'. A blue supergiant roughly 400 parsecs away, it shines with a quarter of a million times the Sun's luminosity, and its spectrum is so steady that it has long served astronomers as a standard anchor for classifying other stars. Fierce stellar winds streaming off its surface light up the surrounding reflection nebula NGC 1990 and strip away its mass at a prodigious rate. Only a few million years old, it is destined to end its short life as a supernova.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 6560604777055249536 resolves in SIMBAD to * alf Gru (Alnair); reverse lookup confirmed.
description: Alnair is the brightest star in Grus, the crane, a hot blue-white main-sequence star about 31 parsecs away. Its name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the bright one', a leftover from when these stars belonged to the tail of the neighbouring Southern Fish before Grus was carved out as a separate constellation. It spins swiftly, with an equatorial velocity above 200 kilometres per second, and radiates several hundred times the Sun's light. Unusually among the bright stars of the southern sky, it has no known companions.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Alnitak Aa (ζ Ori Aa), the O-type supergiant primary; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Alnitak is the easternmost star of Orion's Belt, its Arabic-derived name meaning 'the girdle'. What the eye sees as a single point is really a multiple system dominated by a searingly hot blue supergiant of rare O spectral type, one of the nearest such stars to the Sun, closely attended by a blue companion and a wider third star. Around 400 parsecs away, the primary blazes with a quarter of a million times the Sun's luminosity. The system is embedded in the glowing gas of IC 434 and lies beside the celebrated Flame and Horsehead nebulae.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 1576683529448755328 resolves in SIMBAD to * eps UMa (Alioth); reverse lookup confirmed.
description: Alioth is the brightest star in Ursa Major and, despite its epsilon designation, outshines every other star of the Great Bear; it is the star in the handle of the Big Dipper nearest the bowl. Its name derives from an Arabic phrase for a sheep's fat tail. It is a chemically peculiar Ap star whose strong magnetic field sorts elements into patches across its surface, so that as it rotates every five days its brightness and spectrum ripple slightly, making it the prototype-like member of the Alpha-2 Canum Venaticorum class. Only about 25 parsecs away, it belongs to the Ursa Major Moving Group and long served sailors as one of the standard navigational stars.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Dubhe A (α UMa A), the orange-giant primary; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Dubhe is one of the two Pointer stars of the Big Dipper: the line drawn from it through neighbouring Merak leads the eye to Polaris and true north. Its name is simply the Arabic word for 'bear'. Unlike the eye's impression of a lone orange point about 38 parsecs away, it is really a quadruple system — an orange giant closely orbited by a hotter white companion, with a second pair circling far beyond. Curiously, Dubhe is not a member of the Ursa Major Moving Group that binds most of the Dipper's stars, so the familiar shape is slowly being pulled apart as it drifts the other way.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among Mirfak's identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Mirfak is the brightest star in Perseus, outshining even the constellation's famous variable Algol; its Arabic-derived name means 'the elbow'. A yellow-white supergiant about 155 parsecs away, it has swollen to some fifty times the Sun's diameter and pours out roughly four thousand times its light. Mirfak is the leading light of the Alpha Persei Cluster, a loose swarm of young blue stars easily seen scattered around it in binoculars. Its scale and youth mark it as a massive star that has already begun the swift final chapters of its evolution.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among Wezen's identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Wezen is the third-brightest star in Canis Major, a yellow-white supergiant whose Arabic-derived name means 'the weight'. Though it appears modest to the eye, it lies roughly 500 parsecs away and is truly colossal, swollen to around 190 times the Sun's diameter while holding only fifteen times its mass, giving it an extraordinarily tenuous outer atmosphere. Just twelve million years old, it has already burned through the hydrogen in its core. Within the next hundred thousand years it will balloon into a red supergiant and ultimately detonate as a supernova.

gaiaDr3Note: Structured fields describe the WC8 Wolf-Rayet primary (WR 11); SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for this saturated bright multiple.
description: Gamma Velorum is the brightest and nearest Wolf-Rayet star to the Sun, an exotic, massive object informally nicknamed 'Regor' — 'Roger' spelled backwards, a tribute to Apollo 1 astronaut Roger Chaffee. Its dominant component is a WC8 Wolf-Rayet star, a stripped, blazing-hot stellar core near 57,000 K that has shed its outer layers in a ferocious wind and now shows brilliant emission lines rather than the usual dark absorption features, earning the system the epithet 'Spectral Gem of the Southern Sky'. It orbits a luminous O-type supergiant every eighty days at a distance of roughly 340 parsecs. The Wolf-Rayet star is among the most evolved massive stars known and a candidate future supernova.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among Sargas's identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Sargas lies deep in the tail of Scorpius, near the scorpion's stinger, a yellow-white bright giant about 100 parsecs away. Its name is of ancient Sumerian or Babylonian origin, one of the oldest star names still in use. Having evolved off the main sequence, it has grown to more than twenty-five times the Sun's diameter and shines well over a thousand times as brightly. It rotates quickly enough to be visibly flattened at the poles and is accompanied by a faint close companion.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Kaus Australis — a saturated bright-star hole.
description: Kaus Australis is the brightest star in Sagittarius, marking the base of the archer's bow — its name combines the Arabic word for 'bow' with the Latin for 'southern'. It forms part of the well-known Teapot asterism, sitting at the bottom of the pot's handle. A blue-white giant about 44 parsecs away, it has evolved off the main sequence and radiates some five hundred times the Sun's light. A faint Sun-like companion is thought to orbit it at roughly a hundred astronomical units.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Avior A (ε Car A), the orange-giant primary; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Avior is unusual among bright stars in having no ancient name at all — 'Avior' was coined in the 1930s by Britain's Nautical Almanac Office so that RAF navigators would have a label for it. About 190 parsecs away in Carina, it is a binary pairing a cool, swollen orange giant with a much hotter blue main-sequence companion, their contrasting colours blending to the naked eye. It anchors the False Cross, an asterism of four stars often mistaken for the true Southern Cross, a confusion that has misled more than one navigator. The giant primary has expanded to some 150 times the Sun's diameter.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 1510374147844219904 resolves in SIMBAD to * eta UMa (Alkaid); reverse lookup confirmed.
description: Alkaid is the star at the very tip of the Big Dipper's handle, the last stop as the eye traces the Great Bear's tail. Its name comes from an Arabic phrase, 'the leader of the daughters of the bier', which pictured the three handle stars as mourning maidens following a funeral procession. It is a hot, young blue main-sequence star about 32 parsecs away, spinning rapidly and shining with a blue-white light. Like Dubhe at the opposite end of the Dipper, Alkaid is not a member of the Ursa Major Moving Group, so the two ends of the familiar pattern are drifting in different directions.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Menkalinan Aa (β Aur Aa), the primary of the eclipsing pair; SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR3' (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Menkalinan is the second-brightest star in Auriga after Capella, and its Arabic-derived name means 'the shoulder of the charioteer'. To the eye it is a single white star about 25 parsecs away, but it is really a triple system whose two nearly identical metallic-lined A-type stars orbit each other every four days. Because that orbit is seen almost edge-on, each star periodically eclipses the other, dipping the combined light by a few hundredths of a magnitude. A fainter, more distant companion completes the system.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among Atria's identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Atria is the brightest star in Triangulum Australe, the Southern Triangle, and forms the most conspicuous vertex of that small triangular pattern; its name is simply a contraction of its Bayer designation, Alpha Trianguli Australis. An orange bright giant about 120 parsecs away, it has swollen to well over a hundred times the Sun's diameter as it nears the end of its life. It emits far more X-rays and shows more flaring activity than an ordinary star of its class, a peculiarity astronomers suspect betrays a hidden Sun-like companion orbiting at close range.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Alhena A (γ Gem A), the primary; SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Alhena is the third-brightest star in Gemini and marks the foot of one of the celestial twins; its Arabic-derived name refers to a brand or mark on a camel's neck, from the asterism its early namers saw here. A white subgiant about 34 parsecs away, it has begun to exhaust the hydrogen in its core and is evolving toward becoming a giant. It is a spectroscopic binary: an unseen companion, most likely a Sun-like star, circles it every twelve and a half years on a markedly elongated orbit.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Peacock's bright primary; SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Peacock is the brightest star in Pavo, the peacock, and — like Avior — carries a name invented rather than inherited: Britain's Nautical Almanac Office coined it in the 1930s so that every navigational star in the new air almanac would have a name, borrowing the constellation's title. It is a hot blue-white star about 55 parsecs away, radiating a couple of thousand times the Sun's light. It is a close spectroscopic binary, the two stars circling each other in under twelve days, though the companion has never been directly seen.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Alsephina Aa (δ Vel Aa), the primary of the eclipsing pair; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Alsephina is one of the four stars of the False Cross, an asterism in Vela and Carina that is frequently mistaken for the Southern Cross. Its name derives from an Arabic word for 'the ship', a memory of the vast ancient constellation Argo Navis that once filled this part of the sky. Only about 25 parsecs away, it is a multiple system whose two brightest members orbit each other nearly edge-on, so that they periodically eclipse one another and the star visibly dims every forty-five days — making it one of the brightest eclipsing binaries in the entire sky. A wider third star orbits the close pair over roughly a century and a half.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among Mirzam's identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Mirzam is the bright blue star just west of Sirius in Canis Major, and its Arabic-derived name — 'the Announcer' or 'the Herald' — records exactly that role, since it rises a little before Sirius and so heralds the arrival of the sky's brightest star. It is a hot, massive blue giant about 150 parsecs away, radiating tens of thousands of times the Sun's light. Mirzam is a Beta Cephei variable, its outer layers pulsing every six hours or so to nudge its brightness by a few hundredths of a magnitude — far too subtly for the eye to catch. Despite its great power it is destined to end its short life as a supernova.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Polaris Aa, the Cepheid supergiant; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for the bright primary (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Polaris is the North Star, sitting less than a degree from the north celestial pole so that the whole northern sky appears to wheel around it through the night — a fixed signpost that has guided navigators for centuries. It is not a lone star but the brightest of a triple system, a luminous yellow supergiant circled by a close companion (Polaris Ab) and a wider one (Polaris B). Crucially, Polaris is a classical Cepheid — the nearest of that class to Earth — pulsing over about four days, which makes it a keystone for calibrating the cosmic distance ladder. Oddly, the amplitude of its pulsations has changed markedly over the past century, a restlessness rare among Cepheids.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Alphard (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Alphard is the solitary bright star in the long, faint constellation Hydra, and its Arabic name al-fard, 'the solitary one', captures how conspicuously alone it looks against that empty stretch of sky. An orange giant some 54 parsecs away, it has exhausted the hydrogen in its core and swollen to roughly sixty times the Sun's diameter. The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe called it Cor Hydrae, 'the heart of the water-snake'. Its spectrum shows a mild excess of barium, a chemical fingerprint of fusion products dredged up from deep within an aging star.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Hamal (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Hamal is the brightest star in Aries and marks the ram's head — its name comes straight from the Arabic for 'head of the ram'. About 20 parsecs away, it is an orange giant that has evolved off the main sequence, grown to some fifteen times the Sun's size, and now fuses helium in its core. In antiquity Hamal lay near the vernal equinox, the crossing point that once defined the start of the zodiac, which lent it particular importance to early astronomers. A giant planet, at least a couple of times the mass of Jupiter, is thought to orbit it roughly once a year.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Diphda (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Diphda, also called Deneb Kaitos, is in fact the brightest star in Cetus despite its beta designation, outshining the constellation's nominal alpha. Its odd traditional name derives from an Arabic phrase for 'the second frog', paired with Fomalhaut as the first. An orange giant about 30 parsecs away, it is a red-clump star now fusing helium, having puffed up to nearly twenty times the Sun's radius. It is a notably strong and active X-ray source, betraying a magnetically vigorous outer atmosphere unusual for a star of its type.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Mizar A (ζ UMa A); SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for the bright naked-eye star (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Mizar is the star at the bend of the Big Dipper's handle, famous for its naked-eye companion Alcor — the pair long used as a traditional test of keen eyesight, the 'horse and rider'. Through a telescope Mizar itself splits into two, and it was the first double star ever photographed; each of those two is in turn a spectroscopic binary, making Mizar a quadruple system. It was also the very first spectroscopic binary ever discovered, its components betrayed by the periodic doubling of lines in its spectrum. The white A-type stars lie about 25 parsecs away.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Nunki (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Nunki is the second-brightest star in Sagittarius and forms part of the handle of the Teapot asterism; its name is one of the oldest still in use, taken from a Babylonian designation for the sacred city of Eridu. It is a hot blue main-sequence star roughly 70 parsecs away, several times the Sun's mass and thousands of times its luminosity. Because it sits almost exactly on the ecliptic, Nunki is one of the brightest stars that the Moon and planets can pass in front of, and it is regularly occulted by the Moon. Its blue-white colour marks it as far younger and hotter than the Sun.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Menkent (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Menkent is one of the nearest orange giants to the Sun, lying just 18 parsecs away in Centaurus; its name blends Arabic and Latin roots to mean 'shoulder of the centaur'. Having left the main sequence, it is a red-clump giant about eleven times the Sun's size, quietly fusing helium in its core. Its unusually large proper motion — nearly three-quarters of an arcsecond a year — hints that it did not form locally but drifted in from the outer Milky Way disk. It serves as a handy southern counterpart to the orange giant Pollux in the north.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Alpheratz A (α And A); SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Alpheratz marks one corner of the Great Square of Pegasus even though it officially belongs to Andromeda — a shared star that once carried a Bayer designation in both constellations. Its name comes from an Arabic phrase for 'the navel of the mare'. About 30 parsecs away, it is the brightest known mercury-manganese star: its atmosphere shows bizarre overabundances of mercury, manganese, gallium and other heavy elements, lofted and sorted by radiation in its unusually calm outer layers. It is a close spectroscopic binary, orbited every 97 days by a companion that is itself chemically peculiar.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Mirach (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Mirach is a cool red giant in Andromeda whose name derives from an Arabic word for 'girdle', a memory of its place at the princess's hip. About 60 parsecs away, it has swollen to some eighty times the Sun's diameter and glows a deep orange-red; it is a semiregular variable whose brightness drifts by roughly a tenth of a magnitude. Stargazers prize it as a signpost, since the faint galaxy NGC 404 — nicknamed 'Mirach's Ghost' — hovers just a few arcminutes from the star's glare. A brown-dwarf companion was reported orbiting it in 2023.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 4493746564376875520 resolves in SIMBAD to * alf Oph (Rasalhague), the primary of the pair.
description: Rasalhague is the brightest star in Ophiuchus, the serpent-bearer, and its name means just that — 'the head of the serpent-charmer'. Only about 15 parsecs away, it is a white star spinning so fast, near nine-tenths of its break-up speed, that it is flung into a markedly oblate spheroid, its equator both bulging out and running cooler than its poles. A smaller companion, roughly eight-tenths of the Sun's mass, circles it every nine years or so on an eccentric orbit. That rapid rotation makes the star hard to model as a simple sphere, a recurring theme among the sky's fastest rotators.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Algieba's primary, γ1 Leo (the gold giant); SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for the bright double (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Algieba is one of the finest double stars in the sky for a small telescope, a warm golden pair in the mane of Leo — its name, somewhat confusingly, comes from the Arabic for 'the forehead'. The brighter component is an orange giant about thirty times the Sun's size roughly 40 parsecs away, accompanied by a fainter yellow giant; the two take several centuries to complete an orbit. A massive planet, around ten times the mass of Jupiter, was discovered circling the primary in 2009. To the unaided eye the two stars blend into a single point of golden light.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Kochab (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Kochab is the brighter of the two 'Guardians of the Pole' in Ursa Minor, the pair of stars that circle the celestial pole a short way from Polaris. Around 3000 years ago Kochab lay closest to the pole and served as the pole star of its era, a role Earth's slow precession has since handed to Polaris. It is an orange giant about 40 parsecs away, more than forty times the Sun's radius and several hundred times its brightness. A planet several times the mass of Jupiter is thought to orbit it.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 3011968416163350272 resolves in SIMBAD to * kap Ori (Saiph).
description: Saiph marks the lower-left corner of Orion's great quadrangle, at the giant's knee, yet despite rivalling Rigel in size and power it looks much fainter to us because so much of its ferocious output pours out as invisible ultraviolet light. A blue supergiant roughly 200 parsecs away, its name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the sword of the giant'. It burns at around 26,000 K and shines tens of thousands of times as brightly as the Sun. Like its massive Orion neighbours, Saiph is fated to end its short life as a supernova.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Denebola (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Denebola marks the tail-tuft of Leo — its name is a contraction of an Arabic phrase meaning 'the tail of the lion'. It is a white main-sequence star only about 11 parsecs away, young and hotter than the Sun, and it rotates rapidly. Denebola is a Delta Scuti variable, flickering by a few hundredths of a magnitude many times a day as its surface pulses. It is also girdled by a disk of cool dust, a debris ring that may mark a planetary system in the making.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents the bright primary of the eclipsing triple; Algol was in Gaia DR2 but SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR3' (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Algol, the 'Demon Star', takes its name from the Arabic ra's al-ghul, 'the head of the ogre', and marks the severed head of Medusa in Perseus — a naming that seems to echo an ancient awareness of its eerie behaviour. Every 2.87 days the star fades by more than a full magnitude for several hours, then recovers: it is the prototype eclipsing binary, a close pair in which a dim subgiant periodically passes in front of the bright blue primary. A third star orbits that pair more distantly, making Algol a triple system about 28 parsecs away. Its regular winking, plausibly noticed in antiquity, made it the first star of its class to be understood as an eclipsing binary.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Tiaki (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Tiaki is the second-brightest star in Grus, the crane, and one of the reddest stars easily visible to the naked eye. A cool red giant on the asymptotic branch some 54 parsecs away, it has bloated to more than 150 times the Sun's diameter as it nears the end of its life. It is a semiregular variable, its light drifting by a few tenths of a magnitude as its vast, unstable outer layers pulse over roughly a month. Its name, approved in 2017, comes from a Tuamotuan tradition of Polynesia.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 6127791439360208640 resolves in SIMBAD to * gam Cen (Muhlifain), the combined close double.
description: Muhlifain is a close double star in Centaurus made of two almost identical white stars, so nearly matched that they are difficult to tell apart even at high magnification. To the naked eye they merge into a single point about 40 parsecs away; the pair orbits over roughly eight decades on an elongated path. Its name is confusingly shared with Muliphein in Canis Major, both from the same Arabic root, so the star is often called simply by its Bayer letter, Gamma Centauri. Both components are hot A-type stars just beginning to evolve into giants.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 5300300156538723328 resolves in SIMBAD to * iot Car (Aspidiske).
description: Aspidiske is a luminous white supergiant in Carina, its name coming from a Greek word for 'small shield' — a meaning echoed by its alternative name Turais. It lies far off, around 230 parsecs away, yet shines at second magnitude because it radiates thousands of times the Sun's light. It is one of the four stars of the False Cross, an asterism regularly mistaken for the true Southern Cross, to the frequent confusion of navigators. Around the year 8100 it will drift close to the south celestial pole and briefly serve as a southern pole star.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for Suhail (Lambda Velorum); the saturated bright supergiant falls in a Gaia bright-star gap.
description: Suhail is a cool orange supergiant that marks one of the sails of Vela, the sail lifted from the ancient constellation Argo Navis. Around 210 times the Sun's radius yet only about 32 million years old, it has swelled enormously despite its youth and shines some 8,000 times brighter than the Sun from roughly 170 parsecs away. Its light wanders slowly by a couple of tenths of a magnitude as its bloated outer layers pulse. Its name, from the Arabic 'Suhail al-Wazn', was long shared with several southern stars before the IAU fixed it to Lambda Velorum in 2016.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 1222646935698492160 resolves in SIMBAD to * alf CrB (Alphecca), the system's A-type primary.
description: Alphecca is the jewel of Corona Borealis, the Northern Crown; its name comes from the Arabic 'nayyir al-fakka', 'the bright one of the broken ring', and it is also called Gemma, Latin for 'jewel'. It is an eclipsing binary about 23 parsecs away in which a Sun-like G-star crosses in front of a hot white A-star every 17.4 days, dipping the combined light by roughly a tenth of a magnitude. The bright primary is girdled by a dusty debris disk, a possible planet-forming analogue to the one around Vega. Together the pair resembles a scaled-up, younger version of the Sun and its planetary system.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for the saturated O-type primary Delta Orionis A (Mintaka); the naked-eye point is a hierarchical multiple.
description: Mintaka is the westernmost of the three stars of Orion's Belt, its name from the Arabic 'manṭaqa', meaning 'the belt'. What looks like a single point is really a hierarchical family of at least five stars, dominated by a hot, luminous blue pair — an O-type giant and its companion — that eclipse each other every 5.7 days some 380 parsecs away. It sits almost exactly on the celestial equator, so it rises due east and sets due west for the entire world. In 1904 Johannes Hartmann noticed unmoving calcium lines in Mintaka's spectrum, the first evidence of the cold gas of the interstellar medium drifting between the stars.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 2067518817314952576 resolves in SIMBAD to * gam Cyg (Sadr).
description: Sadr sits at the heart of the Northern Cross, the intersection of the great cross-shaped asterism of Cygnus, the swan; its name is the Arabic word for 'chest'. It is a yellow-white supergiant of enormous size — about 180 times the Sun's radius and 33,000 times its luminosity — lying some 560 parsecs away amid the glowing clouds of the Sadr Region (IC 1318). Massive and short-lived, it is only around 12 million years old and is destined to end as a supernova. Since 1943 its steady spectrum has served as one of the anchor points astronomers use to classify other stars.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes 'Not recovered in Gaia DR2 nor Gaia DR3' for Eltanin (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Eltanin is the brightest star in Draco, the dragon; its name comes from the Arabic 'al-tinnīn', 'the great serpent', and it is also spelled Etamin. An orange giant about 47 parsecs away, it has evolved off the main sequence to some fifty times the Sun's diameter. In 1728 James Bradley, trying to measure its parallax, instead discovered the aberration of starlight — the tiny tilt of a star's apparent position caused by Earth's motion — the first direct proof that Earth orbits the Sun. In roughly 1.5 million years its motion will carry it within about 28 light-years of the Sun, briefly making it the brightest star in the sky.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 418551920284673408 resolves in SIMBAD to * alf Cas (Schedar).
description: Schedar is the brightest star of Cassiopeia, marking the queen's heart in the distinctive 'W' — its name comes from the Arabic 'ṣadr', 'the breast'. It is an orange giant around 70 parsecs away, now fusing helium in its core and swollen to more than forty times the Sun's radius. Long suspected of slight variability by 19th-century observers, it has since held steady, and modern surveys confirm it just outshines its rival Caph as the constellation's alpha. Bayer's alpha label and the two stars' near-equal brightness left early catalogues disagreeing over which was actually the brighter.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 5534788672055388032 resolves in SIMBAD to * zet Pup (Naos).
description: Naos is one of the hottest and most luminous stars visible to the naked eye, a blue supergiant whose surface blazes at some 40,000 K — hot enough to radiate mostly in the ultraviolet. Its name comes from the Greek for 'ship', a remnant of the vast ancient constellation Argo Navis, of which Puppis was the stern. It drives a ferocious stellar wind at around 2,500 kilometres per second, stripping away mass at a prodigious rate, and its true output exceeds a third of a million Suns from about 330 parsecs away. A runaway star tearing across the galaxy, it was likely flung free when a former companion exploded as a supernova.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for the saturated golden primary Gamma-1 Andromedae (Almach); the structured fields describe that bright giant.
description: Almach is the third-brightest star of Andromeda and one of the finest colour-contrast doubles in the sky: a golden-yellow bright giant paired with a fainter blue-green companion, a jewel-like sight in a small telescope. Its name comes from an Arabic word for a small desert cat, the caracal. What the eye sees as a single point is really four stars — the blue companion, Gamma-2, is itself a triple system, first resolved by Wilhelm Struve in 1842. The bright primary described here is a cool K-type giant nearly a hundred times the Sun's radius, lying about 120 parsecs away.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 423018377034969216 resolves in SIMBAD to * bet Cas (Caph).
description: Caph is one of the three bright stars that trace the 'W' of Cassiopeia, its name from the Arabic for 'the palm' of a hand. A yellow-white giant just 17 parsecs away, it has begun to cool and expand as it leaves the main sequence on its way to becoming a red giant. It is one of the brightest Delta Scuti stars in the sky, pulsating gently every two and a half hours to change its brightness by a few hundredths of a magnitude. It also spins rapidly enough to bulge noticeably at its equator, which runs about a thousand degrees cooler than its poles.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 1279798794197267072 resolves in SIMBAD to * eps Boo (Izar), the system's orange-giant primary.
description: Izar is a celebrated double star in Boötes, its telescopic beauty earning it the Latin nickname Pulcherrima, 'the loveliest'. A deep-orange giant is paired with a hot blue-white main-sequence companion, and the vivid colour contrast between them is one of the showpiece sights of the northern sky. The name Izar comes from an Arabic word for a loincloth or girdle, marking the herdsman's waist. The orange primary, now fusing hydrogen in a shell around a spent helium core, has grown to nearly forty times the Sun's size some 70 parsecs away.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 5905821894507108864 resolves in SIMBAD to * alf Lup (Uridim).
description: Uridim is the brightest star of Lupus, the wolf; its name revives the Sumerian 'UR.IDIM', 'mad dog', an ancient title for the constellation. A hot blue giant about 140 parsecs away, it is a Beta Cephei variable, swelling and shrinking every seven hours to ripple its brightness by a few percent. It belongs to the Upper Centaurus–Lupus group of the Scorpius–Centaurus association, the nearest band of young massive stars to the Sun. Weighing some ten solar masses, it is one of the closest stars likely to end its life as a supernova.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for Epsilon Centauri; the saturated blue giant falls in a Gaia bright-star gap.
description: Epsilon Centauri is a hot blue giant in the sprawling constellation Centaurus, one of several bright stars there that never received a proper name. Lying about 130 parsecs away, it is a Beta Cephei variable whose surface pulses every four hours, nudging its brightness by hundredths of a magnitude. It is a young, massive member of the Lower Centaurus–Crux subgroup of the Scorpius–Centaurus association, the closest gathering of hot young stars to the Sun. At more than eight solar masses it burns through its fuel quickly and is bound for a supernova end.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for the saturated B-type primary Delta Scorpii (Dschubba).
description: Dschubba marks the forehead of Scorpius — its name comes from the Arabic 'jabhat', 'the forehead' — and stands at the head of the scorpion's three-star crown. Long a steady second-magnitude star, in the year 2000 it abruptly brightened and began flinging glowing gas from its equator, turning into a Be shell star and briefly altering the familiar shape of the constellation. It is a hot blue subgiant with a companion that swings close every eleven years on a highly elongated orbit, a passage that seems to trigger the outbursts. At its peak it has flared toward first magnitude, far above its usual brightness.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 6026152137856166912 resolves in SIMBAD to * eps Sco (Larawag).
description: Larawag is one of the brightest stars in the body of Scorpius, a mature orange giant just under 20 parsecs away. Its name comes from the Wardaman people of Australia's Northern Territory and means 'clear sighting', referring to a star viewed through the fork of a ceremonial tree; the IAU adopted it in 2017. Having exhausted the hydrogen in its core, the star has cooled and swollen to about thirteen times the Sun's radius. In 2018 it was found to carry a very faint companion of barely a quarter of a percent of its mass, making it a widely separated binary.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for Eta Centauri; the saturated Be star falls in a Gaia bright-star gap.
description: Eta Centauri is a hot, fast-spinning blue star of the Be class, whirling so quickly — around 330 kilometres per second at its equator — that it flings out a flattened disk of gas that orbits it like a miniature ring system. Only a few million years old, it belongs to the Scorpius–Centaurus association, the nearest group of young massive stars to the Sun, and lies about 94 parsecs away. As gas comes and goes from the disk its brightness flickers irregularly, marking it as both a Gamma Cassiopeiae and a Lambda Eridani variable. Massive enough to end as a supernova, it is a vivid example of a star pushed to the edge of stability by its own rotation.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 856096765753549056 resolves in SIMBAD to * bet UMa (Merak).
description: Merak is one of the seven stars of the Big Dipper, forming the bottom of the bowl; its name comes from the Arabic 'al-maraqq', 'the loins' of the great bear. Together with neighbouring Dubhe it makes the famous pair of Pointers — a line drawn through them leads the eye straight to Polaris, the north star. A white main-sequence star about 25 parsecs away, it is a mild chemically-peculiar 'Am' star and is ringed by a disk of dusty debris like those around Vega and Fomalhaut. It belongs to the Ursa Major Moving Group, a loose stream of stars born together and still drifting across the sky in step.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 4993479684438433792 resolves in SIMBAD to * alf Phe (Ankaa).
description: Ankaa is the brightest star in Phoenix, the mythical bird that rises reborn from its own ashes; the name comes from the Arabic 'al-'anqā', 'the phoenix'. An orange giant about 25 parsecs away, it has swelled to some thirteen times the Sun's radius as it ages. It is a spectroscopic binary whose unseen companion completes an orbit every eleven years, betrayed only by the rhythmic shifting of its spectral lines. Though the lucida of its constellation, it is modest beside its brilliant neighbours Achernar and Fomalhaut, leaving it the third-brightest star in that lonely stretch of southern sky.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 5961206940987571200 resolves in SIMBAD to * kap Sco (Girtab), the unresolved spectroscopic pair.
description: Girtab lies in the curl of the scorpion's tail, near the sting; its name is the ancient Sumerian word for 'scorpion', preserved through the Babylonian star lists. It is a hot blue giant some 150 parsecs away, and a spectroscopic binary so tight that its two stars have never been seen apart — their presence is revealed only by the periodic Doppler weaving of the spectrum. The brighter component is a Beta Cephei variable, expanding and contracting several times a day. The star shines on the flag of Brazil, where it stands for the state of Paraíba.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes Epsilon Pegasi (Enif) was not recovered in Gaia DR3 (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Enif is the brightest star in Pegasus, marking the nose of the winged horse; its name is simply the Arabic word for 'nose'. An orange supergiant roughly 210 parsecs away, it is about 180 times the Sun's radius and thousands of times as luminous. Its light usually drifts by small amounts as a slow irregular variable, but it is famous for rare, dramatic flares — on one occasion it was seen to leap briefly to magnitude 0.7, a flash far outshining anything the Sun produces. Such outbursts make this ageing giant a natural laboratory for extreme stellar activity.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD notes Beta Pegasi (Scheat) was not recovered in Gaia DR3 (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Scheat is a cool red giant marking the upper-right corner of the Great Square of Pegasus, and its name comes from an Arabic phrase for the horse's upper arm. About 60 parsecs away, it has swollen past a hundred times the Sun's radius as an ageing asymptotic-giant-branch star, shedding gas and dust into an expanding shell around itself. Its distended surface pulses irregularly, ranking it a semiregular variable that drifts between magnitude 2.3 and 2.8 over roughly six weeks. Cool enough to glow a distinct orange, it is one of the reddest stars easily seen with the naked eye.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for the close A-type binary Eta Ophiuchi (Sabik).
description: Sabik is the second-brightest star of Ophiuchus, the serpent-bearer, yet it never earned a vivid legend — its name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'the preceding one', of forgotten reference. It is in truth a close pair of near-twin white stars, each a little over twice the Sun's mass, circling one another about every 88 years. Lying some 27 parsecs away, the two are so alike that the system shines as a single point to the eye. Because it sits near the ecliptic, Sabik is now and then occulted by the Moon and planets.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 792588939773693568 resolves in SIMBAD to * gam UMa (Phecda), the system's A-type primary.
description: Phecda forms the lower-left corner of the bowl of the Big Dipper, and its name derives from an Arabic phrase for the 'thigh of the bear'. A hot white star about 25 parsecs away, it is a shell star whose rapid spin has wrapped it in a thin disk of its own gas, betrayed by emission lines in its spectrum. A faint companion of roughly four-fifths a solar mass orbits it every twenty years, detected only through the star's tiny astrometric wobble. Like most of the Dipper's stars it belongs to the Ursa Major Moving Group, a stream of stellar siblings drifting together across the sky.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 5605797194566011520 resolves in SIMBAD to * eta CMa (Aludra).
description: Aludra is a brilliant blue supergiant in Canis Major, its name coming from an Arabic term for 'the virgins', a grouping of stars in the great dog's hindquarters. Though it appears only moderately bright, that is because it lies some 600 parsecs away; intrinsically it pours out well over a hundred thousand times the Sun's light. Its outer layers ripple as an Alpha Cygni variable, nudging its brightness by hundredths of a magnitude over a few days. A young star of around nine solar masses, it is burning through its fuel at a furious rate and is destined to end as a supernova.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 2193192137376175488 resolves in SIMBAD to * alf Cep (Alderamin).
description: Alderamin is the brightest star of Cepheus and one of the sky's most rapid rotators, spinning once every twelve hours at nearly 300 kilometres per second — fast enough to bulge visibly at its equator. The name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the right arm'. Only about 15 parsecs away, it is a white star some twice the Sun's mass just beginning to evolve off the main sequence. Because Earth's axis slowly wanders, Alderamin will take its turn as the northern pole star around the year 7500.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 5310393535853560576 resolves in SIMBAD to * kap Vel (Markeb).
description: Markeb is a hot blue star in Vela and one of the four stars of the False Cross, an asterism often mistaken for the true Southern Cross. Its name comes from an Arabic word for 'something to ride', and its spelling was kept deliberately distinct from Markab in Pegasus. About 175 parsecs away, it is a massive subgiant of roughly thirteen solar masses, paired with a hot companion that circles it every 117 days. So heavy a star will run through its life quickly and eventually detonate as a supernova.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 426558460884582016 resolves in SIMBAD to * gam Cas, the prototype Be star.
description: Gamma Cassiopeiae is the central star of Cassiopeia's distinctive W and the prototype of an entire class of variable stars. In 1866 Angelo Secchi found it to be the first star ever seen with bright emission lines, making it the original 'Be' star; it spins so fast — around 450 kilometres per second — that it flings a whirling disk of gas from its equator. As that disk waxes and wanes the star's light flickers unpredictably, and in a 1937 outburst it flared as bright as magnitude 1.6. Some 168 parsecs away and about fifteen times the Sun's mass, it received the formal IAU name Tiansi only in 2025.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 2816504901198512768 resolves in SIMBAD to * alf Peg (Markab).
description: Markab marks the south-western corner of the Great Square of Pegasus, its name coming from an Arabic word for 'the saddle' of the horse. About 41 parsecs away, it is a white subgiant of some three and a half solar masses that has exhausted the hydrogen in its core and is beginning to swell toward its future as a giant. Its spelling is easily confused with Markeb in Vela, and the two names were kept slightly different on purpose. A moderately fast rotator, it shines about 165 times as brightly as the Sun.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 1869302503206674304 resolves in SIMBAD to * eps Cyg (Aljanah).
description: Aljanah is an orange giant marking the eastern wing of Cygnus, the swan, and one arm of the Northern Cross; its name is simply the Arabic word for 'the wing'. Only about 22 parsecs away, it has aged past its hydrogen-burning youth and swollen to some eleven times the Sun's radius, and at nearly ten billion years old it is among the more elderly of the bright stars. It carries a faint red-dwarf companion and, far more distantly, a possible third star on an orbit tens of thousands of years long. It once shared the name Gienah with a star in Corvus before the IAU gave each its own title.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for the saturated multiple system Beta Scorpii (Acrab); HD 144217 is its brightest component.
description: Acrab crowns the head of Scorpius, and its name comes straight from the Arabic word for 'the scorpion'; its alternative title Graffias means 'the claws'. What looks to the eye like a single star is in truth a system of at least five hot blue stars bound in a complex hierarchy, first teased apart when the Moon occulted it and revealed the components winking out one by one. The brightest members are massive stars of fifteen and ten solar masses, blazing tens of thousands of times brighter than the Sun some 120 parsecs away. Sitting almost on the ecliptic, Acrab is regularly occulted by the Moon and occasionally by planets.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 2493390319631956352 resolves in SIMBAD to * omi Cet (Mira A), the pulsating red-giant primary.
description: Mira, 'the Wonderful', is the prototype of the long-period pulsating variables and one of the most famous stars in the sky for its slow vanishing act. Over a cycle of about eleven months it swells and cools, swinging from an easy naked-eye star near third magnitude down below tenth — a hundredfold change in brightness — before slowly rising again. A bloated red giant near the end of its life some 90 parsecs away, it sheds so much gas that it trails a comet-like tail thirteen light-years long, revealed by an ultraviolet survey. A white-dwarf companion, Mira B, orbits it across roughly seventy times the Earth–Sun distance.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 2026116260337482112 resolves in SIMBAD to * bet Cyg A, the amber giant; the id keys the naked-eye system to its brighter component.
description: Albireo, at the beak of Cygnus, is the most celebrated colour-contrast double in the sky: a warm amber giant beside a vivid blue companion, the showpiece toward which countless small telescopes are pointed. The golden primary is itself a close binary, while the blue star is a hot, fast-spinning B-type sun. The two bright stars lie a little over a hundred parsecs away, but Gaia measurements hint that they may merely happen to line up rather than orbit one another. The odd name appears to be a medieval mistranslation of a Greek and Arabic phrase, corrupted through centuries of copying.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 2200153454733285248 resolves in SIMBAD to * del Cep, the prototype Cepheid.
description: Delta Cephei is the prototype of the Cepheid variables, the pulsating supergiants that underpin the cosmic distance ladder. Every 5.37 days it brightens and dims between magnitude 3.5 and 4.4 as its whole body swells and contracts, and the tight link between such a star's pulsation period and its true luminosity — discovered by Henrietta Leavitt — lets astronomers read off distances to far galaxies. A yellow supergiant about 270 parsecs away, its own distance is among the best measured of any Cepheid, pinned to a few percent with the Hubble Space Telescope. It carries a small close companion and a wider hot blue star that shares its motion through space.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 5350358584482202880 resolves in SIMBAD to * eta Car; unusually for so saturated a target, the luminous blue variable does carry a DR3 source.
description: Eta Carinae is one of the most massive and luminous star systems in the galaxy — a primary of around a hundred solar masses paired with a hot, hidden companion, together shining several million times as brightly as the Sun. In the 1840s it flared in the Great Eruption, briefly becoming the second-brightest star in the night sky near magnitude minus one and hurling off the twin-lobed cloud of gas now called the Homunculus Nebula. Some 7,500 light-years away, it sank into obscurity for a century and has since rebrightened to naked-eye visibility around fourth magnitude. Wildly unstable, it is one of the nearest candidates to detonate as a supernova, or even a more violent hypernova.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 2835207319109249920 resolves in SIMBAD to * 51 Peg (Helvetios).
description: 51 Pegasi is an unremarkable-looking Sun-like star in Pegasus with an extraordinary place in history: in 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found a planet circling it, the first world ever confirmed around a normal star like the Sun, an achievement that won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics. That planet, 51 Pegasi b, is a 'hot Jupiter' whipping around its star every 4.2 days — a discovery that overturned assumptions about where giant planets can form and live. The star and its planet were later formally named Helvetios and Dimidium. A little older and richer in metals than the Sun, it lies about 50 light-years away and is only faintly visible to the unaided eye under dark skies.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source for VY Canis Majoris; the deeply embedded hypergiant yields no clean DR3 astrometry.
description: VY Canis Majoris is a red hypergiant in Canis Major and a perennial contender for the largest known star, swollen to roughly 1,400 times the Sun's radius — big enough that, set in the Sun's place, its surface would reach past the orbit of Jupiter. It is shedding matter at a prodigious rate, wrapping itself in a lopsided, glowing nebula of ejected gas and dust that partly hides the star from view. Around 3,800 light-years away, it is deeply unstable and sits near the theoretical size limit for a cool supergiant. It will likely end its short life as a supernova, or perhaps collapse directly into a black hole.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 4152993273702130432 resolves in SIMBAD to V* UY Sct; the red supergiant's DR3 parallax is astrometrically noisy, so its distance and radius stay uncertain.
description: UY Scuti is a red supergiant in Scutum long famous as a candidate for the largest known star. A 2013 study measured it at about 1,700 times the Sun's radius — a size that would swallow the orbit of Jupiter — but better distance estimates since have revised it downward toward 900 solar radii, a vivid lesson in how uncertain stellar sizes really are. Its faint, deeply reddened light varies over roughly two years as the enormous star pulses. Lying several thousand light-years away in a dust-laden reach of the Milky Way, it remains one of the most enormous stars known despite the downward revision.

gaiaDr3Note: Gaia DR3 1220110705972528512 resolves in SIMBAD to V* T CrB, the recurrent-nova binary.
description: T Coronae Borealis, nicknamed the Blaze Star, is a recurrent nova in Corona Borealis — a red giant paired with a heavy white dwarf that steadily draws gas from its companion. Roughly every eighty years enough matter piles onto the white dwarf to trigger a runaway thermonuclear flash, and the normally tenth-magnitude system flares within hours to about second magnitude, briefly rivalling the stars of the Northern Crown. It last erupted in 1866 and 1946, and astronomers widely forecast another outburst in 2024–2026, though as of mid-2026 the star has stayed quiet. Its white dwarf sits near the mass limit above which such a star can explode outright as a supernova.
